title: Opening: Palmer's uncle, Chicago band members, early New Orleans work
summary: Palmer introduces himself, recalls his uncle inspiring him, the Chicago band lineup (Cencere, Dewey, Kepard, Mack), the Dreamland and Royal Garden, then early New Orleans jobs, lawn parties, brass bands, leaving for more money and the vaudeville circuit.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: This is Roy Palmer speaking, and I want to say about the bands, different bands that we have played with in the Orleans and in different towns, different places. I want to explain how I came along in the music game. It was when I was around 15 or 18, I studied music, taking music. From that time I was taking bands, taking bands. I played with regular, and sometimes I played with other bands. I led a lot of bands, bass band and so on. My music was well established because I played and I played with other bands. I played with other bands. I played with other bands. I have an uncle who was a very good musician. That's the thing that caused me to take up music because he used to have a band playing. I was small. I was still very young. I was not a big fan of music. I was not a big fan of music. I was not a big fan of music. I was taking up from what I'd seen him do. I didn't know the instrument, couldn't play the instrument at that time, but this is what I thought. stuff Thank you. And we had several good trombone players. We always used sometimes two trombones in the chorus, you know, see we played together. And we'd used two trombones. And the fellow who played the seventh trombone, he would play baritones sometimes in the orchestra. We also had a very good banjo player. He was nice on banjo. And that was Johnny Cencere. He's from New Orleans also. Who was the clarinetist? The clarinetist was this fellow, Dewey, Lawrence Dewey. He played a C clarinet. And he was very good. He's still down there. Somebody's not going up. That's right. That's right. He's still down there. Well, was Louie Kepard, that's Freddie Kepard's name. Yeah, Louie Kepard. He was the fellow that played a guitar. He played guitar. He was a guitar player. And I don't know whether he changed or anything else, but that's what he usually featured, guitar. And we had several other musicians that came along the line, you know, at that time. Who was your drummer when you came up with? The drummer that we came up with, came here with, was a fellow by the name of Mack. A really young fellow. He must have been about eighteen, fifteen years old. Eighteen. Was it Mack Murray, was it? I don't know his last name, but I know his name was Mack. Yeah, Mack. He was very good, nice drum player. And we used so many different, you know, in the band, we'd use different musicians. At times some fellas wanted to play a gig, some nights would take a different fella, you know, and use them. And use the second trombone. And use the second trombone. I'd use this fella, well John Lindsay was one of the fellas. John Lindsay, he was one of the fellas, and he played with us several times, and two trombones. And George Fields, I played with them. There was, there was, there was first and second trombone. Any place where they had a very large orchestra, they'd use trombone two, two trombones. And these two trombones, one would play first and one would play second. And from that on, in Chicago, we began to build up a nice orchestra, or had nice musicians, or even had the girl playing with us from Chicago. And that was Lily Armstrong, the girl that married Lewis. So we had her playing with us a long while. And afterwards, Joe Oliver came in, and he started his orchestra, and we left the place where we was playing. We were at Dreamlin. And we left the Dreamlin, and we come over to Royal Garden, where, after we stopped playing there, where some of us quit the jobs, and some went one way in different places, you know, went in different directions, different bands, and joined, and that tore the band up. Okay, it's good one again. Tell me about the early days in New Orleans. Well, the early days in New Orleans, we usually played, we had lots of jobs to play through the weekdays, such as funerals and things like that, parties and picnics and other things we'd play, you know. If we'd get out too early, we'd never play it until in the evenings. We'd start around about seven o'clock, and dance or whatever we were playing before would be over with at twelve o'clock. They'd never run any further than twelve or one o'clock at the ladies. They'd let them go sometimes, but they never went over twelve o'clock. They'd start parties and dance. They'd go to the lawn parties and the lawn parties. Usually they do a lot of that work, the lawn party, giving dances out in the open air. What were they like? Well, you have a, it's a large space that they have surrounded with a large high fence, and they use it as a lawn ground for, you know, to dance on a nice lawn, and they'd give a party. They'd give it that way, and the dances would usually be about, there would be about maybe a hundred or two hundred people, you know, in this dance, and it was very good. Did they dance right on the ground? No, they had a pavement. They had a pavement. Some of them had wooden platforms they made, and they used to dance on that. And a good many, lots of times, we played dances on the pavements, you know, but they usually, people didn't go for those dances on the pavement much because they wore out the excuse, and so they usually go for a dance where canvas was laid or wooden floor. And we had a good many bands we played with, such as Tuxedo, Tuxedo Band was very good, Sonny Silistan, he died, but he was very good, and he had a nice band. And the Onward Band, that was good, those brass bands, and they played. Who was in the Onward Band? The Onward Band, George Fields, Manuel Mineta, Manuel Poe, and Ho Johnson, and Hank Johnson, and some of the old timers, you see. And they were very good, they were very good. They had a band that you might say stood up with any band, most of any other band. Most of my playing was with that band, and with the Tuxedo Band, and I used to go out of town and play with other bands, they'd hire me to play. I was supposed to be very good. I was supposed to be very good. So they'd hire me and they'd come and get me, you know, see, and bring me to those places where we had to play. And they'd bring me back home, see. And I had a pretty easy time in the music line. And I arranged a little. Did you do any teaching in New Orleans? Very little, very little I did, because I didn't have time to, from the time after I got in a certain height in the music, that I was able to give instruction and teach, I left, see. I didn't have to leave, but I left because I wanted to make a little money, you know, see. And in that ground, and in that field, they wasn't paying as much money as they played up this way, see. And I just come on up and got my bunch together and we started playing here. Now the first job we played here, it was on the circuit, you might say, the New Orleans Jazz Band, was playing from different theaters, different places. You know, we went to St. Louis, we went to Peoria, and all up Rock Island, and all those big theaters. We had an act, see, you had a small act, you had one woman and one man. And the rest of us, this. And Mabel Elaine, Mabel Elaine, Mabel Elaine was the girl that was on the show, see. She played a, she used a, played a, what do you call it? She played a comedian part, see. She sang there? She sang there, she sang. And we played on the, on the show. Then we went from there to St. Louis, and different places, Rock Island, Highway, and all, all different short trips, not too long, not too far away. We was working for Locales and Krause then at that time, Lee Krause and Mitchell Locales. They used to have the Broadway theater, at Broadway and 4200 Broadway. There was a theater over there. In Chicago? Yeah, in Chicago. They used to have that, they had that theater in charge. And most of our playing we did was, when we hung up, we stopped there and played there, and then we stayed around Chicago until we got another thing. You mentioned the Raleans, they didn't pay much. What did they, used to pay the dance? They run around about three or four dollars. They wasn't paying so much at night, see. At that time the scale was low anyway, see. And we didn't make so much.
